title: Is this a one-way door or a two-way door?
hook: Most decisions get the same heavy process, even though only a few deserve it.
coreIdea: In his 2015 shareholder letter, Jeff Bezos described Type 1 decisions as consequential and nearly irreversible, one-way doors, and Type 2 decisions as changeable and reversible, two-way doors. Type 1 decisions deserve slow, careful deliberation. Type 2 decisions can be made quickly by a person or small group, because if you walk through and dislike the room, you walk back. The failure he warned about is treating Type 2 decisions with Type 1 heaviness.
whyItMatters: Applying heavy approval to reversible choices slows the whole team and saves almost no risk.
example: Illustrative: changing the wording of a macro reply is a two-way door; the lead can try it for a week and revert. Switching ticketing platforms, with data migration and retraining, is a one-way door that justifies a proper review.
reflectionQuestion: Which decision waiting for your sign-off right now is actually reversible within a week?
suggestedAction: For each item in your approval queue, write 'one-way' or 'two-way' beside it and hand back every two-way item to the owner to decide.

source.title: 2015 Letter to Shareholders
source.author: Jeff Bezos (Amazon)

deeper: Reversibility is a matter of cost, not yes or no. A decision is a two-way door when undoing it is cheap and fast. Some choices look reversible but are not, such as a public promise to a key customer or a policy people have already adapted to. Bezos also noted that organisations drift toward one-size-fits-all heavy process; the habit to build is asking the door question first, before choosing how much analysis to do.
simpleExplanation: If you can easily undo a choice, decide fast; if you can't undo it, slow down.

keyConcepts.label: Match the process to the door

title: And then what? Thinking one step further
hook: The first-order effect of a decision is usually the one everyone already sees.
coreIdea: First-order thinking asks what happens next. Second-order thinking asks: and then what, and who reacts? Investor Howard Marks calls the related idea second-level thinking in The Most Important Thing (2011): the obvious view is shared by everyone, so it rarely gives an edge. For a manager, a decision is not just its direct result but the behaviour it teaches people to adopt in response.
whyItMatters: Many policies that look sensible on day one produce the opposite of what you wanted by month three.
example: Illustrative: a lead cuts average handle time targets to clear a backlog. First-order effect: cases close faster. Second-order effect: agents close cases early, customers reopen them, and the backlog returns with a worse reputation.
reflectionQuestion: Think of your last policy change. What did people on your team learn to do differently because of it?
suggestedAction: Before announcing your next change, write down two things people will do in response, and one way each could backfire.

source.title: The Most Important Thing
source.author: Howard Marks

deeper: Marks wrote about investing, where 'second-level thinking' means forming a view different from the consensus and better. The management version borrows the habit rather than the claim: trace the chain of reactions. Limits: you cannot predict every ripple, and endless chains lead to paralysis. Stop at two or three steps, prefer small reversible trials, and watch for the specific reaction you most fear.
simpleExplanation: Before you decide, ask what happens next and how people will react to that.

title: The vivid case vs the boring base rate
hook: A specific story about this customer can make you ignore what usually happens.
coreIdea: Base-rate neglect is the tendency to focus on the details of a particular case and underweight how common that outcome is overall. Kahneman and Tversky documented it in their 1973 work on the psychology of prediction. The counterintuitive part: even when a case looks like a classic example of something rare, the rare explanation is still often less likely than a dull common one. Start with the base rate, then adjust for the case-specific evidence.
whyItMatters: Escalating or diagnosing on a convincing story, while ignoring how rarely it is true, burns engineering time and customer trust.
example: Illustrative: a device goes offline and the customer insists it is a firmware bug. If, in your history, most offline cases turn out to be power or SIM issues, check those first, then adjust upward if the logs show the firmware signature.
reflectionQuestion: What is the base rate of the most common root cause in your queue, and do your agents know it?
suggestedAction: Pull the last 50 closed escalations, count root causes, and share the top three percentages with your team as the starting guess for new cases.

source.title: On the psychology of prediction
source.author: Daniel Kahneman & Amos Tversky

deeper: A base rate is only useful if it comes from a comparable group, so choose the reference class with care: all offline cases, or offline cases on this hardware revision? Base rates are a starting point, not a verdict. A strong, specific signal, such as a known error code in the logs, should move you far from the prior. The error is not using specifics; it is letting them replace the prior entirely.
simpleExplanation: Before you believe the exciting explanation, ask how often it is really the cause.

keyConcepts.label: Base rate is how common something is overall
Start with the base rate then adjust

title: The fence you want to remove
hook: "I can't see why it's there" is not a reason to tear it down.
coreIdea: In The Thing (1929), G. K. Chesterton described a reformer who finds a fence across a road and wants it cleared away because he sees no use for it. The wiser reply: go and find out why it was put up, and then you may remove it. The principle is not 'never change things'. It is that not understanding a rule's purpose is a fact about you, not evidence that the rule has no purpose.
whyItMatters: Removing an inherited process you don't understand can silently bring back the problem it was created to stop.
example: Illustrative: a new manager finds that every firmware-related escalation needs a device log bundle before it goes to engineering, and wants to drop it as red tape. The rule exists because engineers once spent days chasing cases with no logs.
reflectionQuestion: Which rule in your team do you find pointless, and what have you done to learn its history?
suggestedAction: Pick one process step you want to remove. Ask two long-serving people why it was introduced before you change it.

source.title: The Thing: Why I Am a Catholic
source.author: G. K. Chesterton

deeper: What would you do? Treat it as a short investigation, not a veto: find who added the rule, what incident prompted it, and whether the original cause still exists. If the reason is gone, remove the rule confidently, ideally as a reversible trial. If nobody can say why it exists, that is itself information, and a time-boxed experiment is safer than a permanent deletion. The fence principle can also be misused as an excuse to never change anything.
simpleExplanation: Before you remove an old rule, find out why somebody made it.

keyConcepts.label: Not seeing a use is not proof of no use
Remove it once the reason is gone

title: Your dashboard is not your customer
hook: Every report is a drawing of reality, and drawings leave things out.
coreIdea: Alfred Korzybski's line, "the map is not the territory", reminds us that any model, report or metric is a simplified representation of the thing itself. A map is useful because it leaves details out, and dangerous when we forget that it did. In support, the CSAT score, the SLA report and the ticket status are maps. The customer's actual experience, and the real state of the device, is the territory.
whyItMatters: When the report and reality disagree, a leader who trusts the report makes confident, wrong decisions.
example: Illustrative: the dashboard shows an escalation as 'In progress with engineering' for nine days. The status was set on day one; nobody has touched it since. The map says active, the territory says stalled.
reflectionQuestion: Which report do you trust most, and when did you last compare it to a raw case or customer call?
suggestedAction: Pick one dashboard number and trace three underlying cases by hand to see what the number hides.

quote.text: The map is not the territory.
quote.note: The phrase is associated with Korzybski's 1931 talk and his 1933 book Science and Sanity; it is often quoted in slightly different wordings.

source.title: Science and Sanity
source.author: Alfred Korzybski

deeper: Maps are not useless; the point is to know what yours omits. Ask what the model assumes, what it cannot see, and how stale it is. Walking the territory, by reading raw cases, listening to calls or visiting a customer site, is the cheapest correction. This idea overlaps with Goodhart's law: when a measure is targeted, it drifts further from the thing it was meant to represent.
simpleExplanation: A report is only a picture of what is really happening, and pictures miss things.

title: Ask how to guarantee failure
hook: Sometimes the quickest way to a good process is to design the worst one first.
coreIdea: Inversion means solving a problem backwards: instead of asking how to achieve a goal, ask what would guarantee its failure, then avoid that. Charlie Munger popularised the habit, quoting the mathematician Carl Jacobi's advice to 'invert, always invert'. It works because people can usually list ways things go wrong more easily and more honestly than they can describe ideal success. The list of failures becomes a checklist of things to prevent.
whyItMatters: Negative thinking is cheap, specific and often exposes risks that positive planning misses.
example: Illustrative: to improve escalation handling, the team lists how to guarantee a terrible outcome, then turns each into a rule.
reflectionQuestion: If you wanted your team's best engineer to resign this year, what would you do? Are you doing any of it?
suggestedAction: Take one goal for this quarter and spend ten minutes listing the ways to guarantee failing it. Pick the top two to remove.
checklist: Escalate without logs, device ID or steps tried
Never tell the customer who owns the case now
Let cases wait in a queue nobody is watching
Change the priority without telling the other team
Close the case before the customer confirms the fix

source.title: Original synthesis of the inversion habit attributed to Carl Jacobi and popularised by Charlie Munger

attribution: 'Invert, always invert' is attributed to Carl Jacobi and is widely quoted by Charlie Munger.
deeper: Inversion is close to the pre-mortem but needs no group and no imagined future: you simply flip the question. Use it when a goal feels vague, such as better customer experience, because the failures are concrete and checkable. Its limit is that avoiding every failure does not by itself create success, so pair it with a positive picture of what good looks like.
simpleExplanation: To get good results, first work out how you would get terrible ones, then avoid those things.

title: Why your 30-minute meeting costs an engineer a morning
hook: Managers cut their day into hours. Makers need half-days.
coreIdea: In his 2009 essay, Paul Graham contrasted two schedules. The manager's day is chopped into one-hour slots, and a meeting is just another slot. The maker's schedule, for people who build things like code or analysis, runs in half-day units, because deep work needs unbroken blocks. A single meeting in the middle of an afternoon can break it in two, and neither half is big enough to do the hard work.
whyItMatters: If you manage people who build or investigate, your calendar habits quietly decide how much deep work they get.
example: Illustrative: a support leader books a 4 pm status call with engineers working on a firmware escalation. Engineers start winding down at 3:30 because there is not enough time to begin anything hard. A manager sees a thirty-minute call; the engineer loses the afternoon.
reflectionQuestion: Who reports to you or works with you on a maker schedule, and when did you last put a meeting in the middle of their day?
suggestedAction: Move one recurring meeting with engineers or analysts to the start or end of the day, or replace it with a written update.

source.title: Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule
source.author: Paul Graham

deeper: Many roles are mixed. A support lead may be a manager at 10 am and a maker when writing an RCA at 3 pm. Graham's point is that the two modes conflict when they meet, and the fix is explicit rather than moral: cluster meetings, protect blocks, and tell collaborators which mode you or they are in. For urgent incidents the maker schedule should yield, but only for real urgency, not habit.
simpleExplanation: A short meeting in the middle of someone's work block can ruin the whole block.

title: Work expands to fill the time you give it
hook: A tongue-in-cheek line from 1955 explains why deadlines work.
coreIdea: C. Northcote Parkinson opened a humorous essay in The Economist in 1955 with the observation that work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion. His target was the growth of bureaucracies, not individual time management, but the idea has stuck as a rule of thumb: a task given a week tends to take a week. A tighter, realistic deadline often shrinks effort without shrinking quality, because it forces choices about what matters.
whyItMatters: Generous deadlines can quietly lower the pace of work without anyone deciding to slow down.
example: Illustrative: a weekly SLA breach report is always 'due Friday' and always gets compiled on Friday afternoon. When the lead asks for it by Wednesday noon, it takes the same two hours and is no worse.
reflectionQuestion: Which recurring task of yours takes exactly as long as its deadline allows?
suggestedAction: Pick one recurring task and halve its time slot for the next two weeks. Note whether the result suffers.

quote.text: Work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion.
quote.note: It was a satirical essay about civil-service staffing, not an empirical study of individual productivity.

source.title: Parkinson's Law
source.author: C. Northcote Parkinson

deeper: Treat it as a hypothesis to test, not a law of nature. Cutting time works for tasks with slack, such as reports and routine reviews. It backfires for complex or creative work, where rushing creates rework, and for people already overloaded. The sensible use is to set deadlines from a realistic estimate of effort, not from habit or from the calendar's convenient slots.
simpleExplanation: If you give yourself a week for something, it will usually take a week, even if it needed two days.

keyConcepts.label: Work stretches to fit the time

title: Did Eisenhower really invent the Eisenhower matrix?
hook: The famous urgent-important grid has a murkier origin story than its name suggests.
coreIdea: Myth: Eisenhower designed a four-box urgent-versus-important matrix for running his day. Reality: the grid was popularised later, notably by Stephen Covey in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), and linked to Eisenhower through a remark about urgent and important tasks that he attributed to someone else. The tool itself is still useful: sort work into urgent and important, important only, urgent only, and neither, then give most of your attention to the important ones before they become urgent.
whyItMatters: Good tools are worth using, but a famous name on a tool is not evidence that it works.
example: Illustrative: a support lead's day is filled with urgent pings from other teams. Plotting a week on the grid shows that coaching and root-cause work, both important and non-urgent, got no time at all.
reflectionQuestion: What important task has not been urgent yet but will become a fire if you ignore it for a month?
suggestedAction: List this week's tasks in the four boxes. Block one hour for the most valuable item in the important, non-urgent box.

source.title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
source.author: Stephen R. Covey

attribution: The quoted idea is usually tied to a 1954 Eisenhower speech in which he referred to a statement by a former university president; check primary sources before repeating the attribution.
deeper: The common mistake is to treat 'urgent' as meaning 'someone is shouting'. Urgency is often about other people's priorities, which makes the grid useful for spotting where your time is being allocated by interruption. A limit is that it assumes you can judge importance, which needs a clear goal. If you cannot say what is important, no grid will help.
simpleExplanation: Sort your tasks by what matters and what is pressing, and don't spend all your time on things that just shout loudest.

keyConcepts.label: Four boxes of urgent and important
Origin is more complicated than the name

title: Priority is impact times urgency, not who shouted
hook: Three ways to order a queue give three very different Mondays.
coreIdea: A queue can be ordered by arrival time, by customer importance, or by a priority matrix. ITIL's incident-management approach sets priority from impact, how many people or how much business is affected, and urgency, how soon it hurts. First-come-first-served is fair but ignores harm. Ordering by account size rewards the loudest or biggest customer. The matrix is harder to run but forces the question that matters: how bad, and how soon?
whyItMatters: Without an explicit rule, priority drifts to whoever escalates loudest, and real emergencies wait behind them.
example: Illustrative: a 40-vehicle fleet reports cameras offline overnight, while a large account asks about a billing line. Arrival order puts billing first; an impact-urgency check puts the offline fleet first.
reflectionQuestion: When two cases compete for the next hour of your best engineer, how is that decided today, and does everyone know the rule?
suggestedAction: Write a 3x3 impact-by-urgency grid with one real case example in each cell, and use it in your next queue review.

source.title: ITIL Service Operation (incident management priority matrix)
source.author: AXELOS / Cabinet Office

deeper: The matrix needs guardrails. Define impact and urgency in observable terms such as number of devices, safety implications or contractual deadline, so two agents classify the same case the same way. Review priority again as facts change. Treat contractual customer tiers as an input to impact rather than a separate queue, or the top tier will crowd out genuinely severe problems elsewhere.
simpleExplanation: Decide what to work on first by how many people are hurt and how soon, not by who asks loudest.

title: The escalation engineering can act on in five minutes
hook: Most escalation delays are caused by what is missing, not by what is wrong.
coreIdea: An escalation is a hand-off of work between people with different context. Engineers can only act when they can reproduce, find or reason about the problem without going back to ask. A good escalation answers a standard set of questions up front: what the customer sees, what the expected behaviour was, the identifiers needed to find the case, what has been tried, and what is needed from engineering by when.
whyItMatters: Every clarifying question bounces the case back through the queue and can add a day to resolution.
example: Illustrative: 'Customer says device offline, please check' takes three round trips. 'Device ID, offline since 02:10 IST, power and SIM verified, last log upload 01:58, 40 vehicles affected, need root cause before 6 pm' can be picked up immediately.
reflectionQuestion: What question does engineering ask most often when an escalation arrives, and why is it not already answered?
suggestedAction: Ask engineering for their top three recurring clarifying questions and add them as mandatory fields in your escalation template.
checklist: What the customer sees, in their words, and what they expected
Identifiers: account, device or case IDs, timestamps with time zone
What was already checked or tried, and the result
Scope and impact: how many users or devices, any safety or contract issue
The ask and the deadline: what exactly engineering must do and by when

source.title: Original synthesis

deeper: A template is only as good as its enforcement and its feedback loop. Review a sample of rejected or slow escalations monthly and ask what field would have prevented the delay. Avoid making the template so long that agents fill it with filler to get through. Fewer, better fields that engineering actually uses will beat a long form.
simpleExplanation: Give engineers everything they need in the first message so they don't have to ask.

keyConcepts.label: Include what, who, tried, scope, ask

title: Handing over the status, not the state
hook: The most dangerous sentence at shift change is 'it's all in the ticket'.
coreIdea: A common mistake at shift or owner change is passing on a status ('waiting on engineering') rather than the state of the situation: what has been tried, what is suspected, what the customer was told, what is due next and who is committed to it. The Google SRE book (2016) stresses explicit incident hand-offs in which the incoming person is told, and acknowledges, that they now own it. Implicit ownership is how things fall between shifts.
whyItMatters: A fumbled hand-off repeats work, contradicts what the customer was told, and quietly stalls the case.
example: Illustrative: the day shift hands over a device-offline escalation with the note 'engineering looking'. Night shift does not know that the customer was promised an update by 9 pm, so no update goes out and the customer escalates.
reflectionQuestion: At your last shift change, could the incoming person state who owned each open critical case without opening the ticket?
suggestedAction: Add three lines to your hand-off note: what the customer was promised and when, what to do next, and 'owner now: name'.

source.title: Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems (chapter on managing incidents)
source.author: Betsy Beyer et al. (eds.)

deeper: Flagged for source check: the SRE book's exact wording on hand-offs should be confirmed against the chapter before quoting. Practically, a good hand-off is a short conversation, not just a document, because the receiver can ask what the note leaves out. Keep the format identical every shift so gaps are obvious, and keep a short list of 'cases at risk' separate from the full queue.
simpleExplanation: When you pass work on, tell the next person everything they need and make sure they know it is theirs now.

title: Who owns the customer while engineering fixes the bug?
hook: Two reasonable answers lead to two very different support organisations.
coreIdea: Once a customer problem is traced to a product defect, a hand-off happens. One view: support keeps ownership of the customer relationship until the customer confirms resolution, and engineering owns the fix. The other view: once engineering accepts the case, they own it, and support should step back to avoid duplicate chasing. Each avoids a real failure, but both create a different one when the boundary is unclear.
whyItMatters: Ambiguous ownership during defects is where customers get contradictory updates, or none at all.
example: Illustrative: a firmware bug affects 200 devices. If support disowns the case, no one tells the customer a fix is delayed. If support micromanages the engineering thread, engineers spend their time answering status pings.
reflectionQuestion: For your last long-running engineering escalation, who told the customer about each delay, and was it the same person every time?
suggestedAction: Write a one-line rule for your team: 'Support owns __; engineering owns __; status updates come from __ every __ days.' Check it against your two oldest open escalations.

source.title: Original synthesis of common support-engineering ownership models

contrarian.question: Should support keep owning the customer after a case is handed to engineering?
established: The customer experiences one company and needs one clear voice for updates.
Engineers need uninterrupted time to diagnose and fix the defect.
Unclear ownership creates gaps in both communication and the fix.

positions.label: Support keeps the customer
positions.claim: Support owns the customer relationship until the customer confirms resolution.
evidence: Support holds the customer context, history and contact channel.
Engineers are not set up to manage expectations or communicate on a schedule.
positions.interpretation: Support as the single voice prevents silence and contradictory messages, and engineering can focus on the fix.

positions.label: Engineering owns it
positions.claim: Once engineering accepts the case, they own the outcome, and support steps back.
evidence: Ownership split across two teams can lead to each assuming the other is chasing.
Support may relay updates it does not fully understand, adding delay and distortion.
positions.interpretation: Single ownership of the problem, with support handling only the customer conversation on request, reduces hand-off friction.

contrarian.opinion: Editorial view: split by role, not by case. Engineering owns the fix and technical status; support owns the customer communication and the closure check, on a fixed update schedule.
unresolved: How much this depends on organisation size and engineering's capacity to handle customer contact.
Whether the split works equally for safety-critical issues and routine defects.
contrarian.balanceNote: Both positions rest on practitioner experience rather than rigorous studies. The right model depends on your product, team size and customer expectations.

deeper: The practical test is whether a customer can answer three questions from one source: what is happening, who is working on it, and when they will hear next. Whichever model you choose, write it down, name a person rather than a team for each role, and review it after any escalation that went badly.
simpleExplanation: When a bug is being fixed, decide clearly who talks to the customer and who fixes the problem.

keyConcepts.label: Split by role with a clear update owner

title: Is this week's spike a signal or just noise?
hook: Reacting to every blip trains a team to chase ghosts.
coreIdea: Any process produces natural variation: some weeks have more tickets, some fewer, with no real cause. Walter Shewhart's control charts, introduced in 1931, separate that routine variation from genuine signals by drawing limits around the process average. A point inside the limits is usually noise and should not trigger an investigation. A point far outside, or a sustained run on one side, deserves a cause. Treating noise as signal creates busywork and demoralises people.
whyItMatters: Leaders who chase every wobble burn effort on ghosts, and miss slow drifts that matter.
example: Illustrative: weekly firmware-related escalations run between 18 and 30 for months. A week with 31 prompts a team-wide review that finds nothing. Three weeks later, a steady rise to 40 over five weeks, which is a real shift, is spotted late because attention was spent on the earlier blip.
reflectionQuestion: What was the last 'spike' you investigated, and would it have been within normal variation?
suggestedAction: Plot 20 weeks of one key metric with its average and a band of normal range. Decide in advance what counts as a signal before the next review.

source.title: Economic Control of Quality of Manufactured Product
source.author: Walter A. Shewhart

deeper: The control-chart idea was developed for manufacturing, and its statistical assumptions, such as stable, roughly independent measurements, do not hold perfectly for support queues, where volume is affected by releases and seasons. Use it as a disciplined habit rather than an exact test: know your normal range, write down your signal rules in advance, and look for runs and trends as well as single outliers.
simpleExplanation: Numbers wobble for no reason; learn the normal wobble so you only react when something real changes.

keyConcepts.label: Define limits for what counts as a signal

title: Is your coaching based on cases or impressions?
hook: Feedback without a case in hand is an opinion the agent can argue with.
coreIdea: Coaching works better when it points to specific, reviewed cases instead of general impressions. A sampled case lets you and the agent look at the same evidence: what the customer wrote, what the agent replied, what the outcome was. It moves the conversation from 'you are slow on escalations' to 'on this case the log request came on day three; what made that hard?' Use the self-check below to see how grounded your coaching is.
whyItMatters: Impression-based feedback feels personal and is easy to dispute; case-based feedback feels like a shared investigation.
example: Illustrative: a lead tells an agent his escalations are weak. After reading five of his cases together, they both see he never states the customer impact, so engineering deprioritises them. The fix is specific and the agent agrees with it.
reflectionQuestion: Which agent have you given the most vague feedback to recently, and which case would make it specific?
suggestedAction: Before your next one-to-one, pick two recent cases for that agent, one strong and one weaker, and open both in the meeting.
checklist: Did I read at least two of this agent's cases in full before the last coaching conversation?
Can I name one specific thing they did well, with the case it happened in?
Did I ask what they were thinking at the decision point, before offering my view?
Did we agree one concrete behaviour to try on the next case?
Do I sample cases for everyone, not only the people I am worried about?

source.title: Original synthesis

deeper: Count your yes answers, but pay most attention to the last question. Case sampling used only on struggling agents feels like surveillance, and sampling that only looks for faults teaches people to hide cases. Share the sampling method openly, include strong work, and keep case reviews separate from scoring so the conversation can stay curious.
simpleExplanation: Use real examples when you give feedback so you and the person are looking at the same thing.

title: Sorting support tasks for AI: cost of error and checkability
hook: The question is not 'can AI do it' but 'what happens when it is wrong, and who will notice?'
coreIdea: To decide where AI belongs in a support workflow, score each task on two things. First, the cost of an error: is it cheap to undo, or does it reach the customer or touch money? Second, checkability: can a person verify the output quickly against a source? Low cost and easy to check, such as summarising a long case thread, suits automation. High cost and hard to check, such as promising a delivery date, needs a human decision.
whyItMatters: Teams that start with 'what can AI do' tend to automate the risky steps first because they look impressive.
example: Illustrative: summarising a 60-message escalation thread is cheap to verify by skimming. Auto-sending root-cause explanations to customers is costly and hard to verify, so a person approves each one.
reflectionQuestion: Which task would you automate first if only errors you could catch within a minute were allowed?
suggestedAction: List ten recurring support tasks and mark each as high or low on error cost and checkability. Pilot AI only on the low-cost, easy-to-check ones.

source.title: Original synthesis

deeper: Four quadrants follow. Cheap and checkable: automate, and sample. Cheap and hard to check: automate with spot audits. Costly and checkable: let AI draft and a human approve with the evidence visible. Costly and hard to check: keep human-led, with AI at most as a research aid. Revisit the scoring as you collect data, because measured error rates beat gut feel.
simpleExplanation: Let AI do jobs where mistakes are cheap and easy to spot, and keep people in charge where mistakes are costly or hidden.

title: Escalation quality starts with whether it feels safe to ask
hook: Agents who fear looking incompetent escalate late, or never.
coreIdea: Psychological safety, a term from Amy Edmondson's research, is the shared belief that it is safe to raise questions and admit uncertainty. In a support team it shows up in a concrete place: the decision to escalate. Where it is low, agents hold cases too long to avoid looking weak or escalate in a panic to avoid blame. Where it is high, they escalate early, with clear context, because asking for help is treated as part of the job.
whyItMatters: Late escalations and vague escalations are often symptoms of fear, which no template can fix.
example: Illustrative: a junior agent sits on a recurring camera-offline case for four days because the last person who escalated was told they 'should have checked more'. When the case finally reaches engineering, the customer has already complained twice.
reflectionQuestion: What is the first thing you say when an agent escalates a case you think they could have solved?
suggestedAction: In your next team meeting, thank someone publicly for an early escalation, including one that turned out to be unnecessary.

bridge.insight: Psychological safety is what makes escalation timing and quality honest: agents who are not punished for asking for help escalate earlier and describe the problem more candidly.

source.title: Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams
source.author: Amy C. Edmondson

deeper: Applying Edmondson's work to escalations is an interpretation, not a finding from her studies. Keep accountability in the picture: safety does not mean every escalation is good. Review them without blame, to improve the template and training, and track the pattern of late escalations by team and manager rather than by individual agent.
simpleExplanation: If people are afraid of being blamed, they wait too long to ask for help.

keyConcepts.label: Psychological safety lets people ask for help

title: Toyota's five whys, and where the method runs out
hook: Asking why five times finds a cause. It does not promise to find the cause.
coreIdea: The five whys technique is associated with Taiichi Ohno and the Toyota Production System: when a problem occurs, ask why repeatedly until you reach a cause you can act on. Its strength is simplicity and its weakness is the same: it follows one chain, so different people can reach different roots, and it can stop at a convenient answer such as 'human error'. Use it as a start, and widen the lens when several things contributed.
whyItMatters: A single-chain RCA can end with a person to blame while the system that made the failure easy stays untouched.
example: Ohno's own example in Toyota Production System (1988) traces a stopped machine back through several causes to a missing strainer, not simply a blown fuse. The lesson is to keep asking until a systemic fix, not just a repair, appears.
reflectionQuestion: In your last postmortem, at which 'why' did the team stop, and who decided that was deep enough?
suggestedAction: Take a recent incident and branch the chain: at each 'why', write every plausible cause, not just one, then decide which ones to test.

source.title: Toyota Production System: Beyond Large-Scale Production
source.author: Taiichi Ohno

deeper: Flagged for source check: confirm the exact details of Ohno's machine example against the book before repeating them. Beyond that, 'five' is a rule of thumb, not a target. Stop when you reach something you can change and verify. Good practice includes asking 'why did the system allow this?' rather than 'who did this?', and testing each causal link with evidence, not agreement in the room.
simpleExplanation: Keep asking why until you find something you can fix, but remember there may be more than one cause.

title: Failures line up through the holes in several defences
hook: Serious incidents rarely come from one big mistake.
coreIdea: James Reason's Swiss cheese model, from Human Error (1990), pictures each defence in a system as a slice of cheese with holes. Holes are weaknesses: a missing check, a rushed review, an unclear hand-off. Any single slice usually stops the problem. An incident happens when holes in several layers line up. The practical consequence is to strengthen many layers a little, and to stop treating the last person to touch the problem as the cause.
whyItMatters: Fixing only the final hole, usually a person, leaves the other layers just as thin for next time.
example: Illustrative: a faulty firmware build reaches 300 devices. Testing missed one hardware variant, the release checklist did not require staged rollout, monitoring alerts were set too high, and the support runbook had no rollback step. Fixing only one of them would not have prevented it.
reflectionQuestion: For your most recent incident, how many separate layers failed, and which fix did you assign to each?
suggestedAction: For one past incident, draw the layers it passed through and mark each hole. Choose the cheapest layer to strengthen first.

source.title: Human Error
source.author: James Reason

deeper: Reason distinguished active failures, committed by people at the sharp end, from latent conditions built into the system by design, scheduling or management decisions. Latent conditions can sit dormant for years. The model is a metaphor, not a measurement: it helps you ask better questions but does not tell you how many layers are enough or how to weigh them.
simpleExplanation: Accidents happen when weaknesses in several safeguards line up at once, so fix many safeguards, not just one.

keyConcepts.label: Layers of defence each have holes

title: Little's law: why your backlog is arrivals times wait
hook: One short formula explains why a queue grows when work waits longer.
coreIdea: John D. C. Little proved in 1961 that, for a stable system, the average number of items inside it equals the average arrival rate times the average time each item spends there: L = λW. For a support queue, open cases equal cases arriving per day multiplied by average days to resolve. If arrivals stay constant, the only way to reduce the open backlog is to shorten how long each case stays in the system, including waiting time between teams.
whyItMatters: It shifts the conversation from 'we need more people closing cases' to 'where are cases waiting?'
example: Illustrative: 40 new escalations arrive per day and each stays open for an average of 3 days, so about 120 are open at any time. Cutting average time to 2 days, for instance by removing a hand-off wait, reduces the open count to about 80 without anyone working faster.
reflectionQuestion: Of your average resolution time, how much is active work and how much is waiting for someone else?
suggestedAction: Take your last 30 closed escalations and split each one's elapsed time into 'being worked' and 'waiting'. Find the largest wait stage.

source.title: A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = λW
source.author: John D. C. Little

deeper: The law holds for long-run averages in a stable system, where what arrives eventually leaves. It says nothing about the shape of waits: a few very old cases can hide inside a healthy average, so also look at the oldest items and the distribution. If arrivals exceed completions for long, the system is not stable and the formula describes a growing backlog, not a steady one.
simpleExplanation: The number of open cases depends on how many come in and how long each one stays open.

keyConcepts.label: L = arrival rate times time in system
